Theosis Metabolic Simulator

See where your body is headed, in fat and muscle, not just pounds. Five short steps. Every answer comes with a sensible default, so you can click straight through and fine-tune later.

Simple keeps it short. Advanced adds training details, measured numbers and manual macros. You can switch any time.

    Body fat

    How do you know your body fat?

    U.S. Navy tape method (Hodgdon & Beckett, 1984). Measure snug, not tight, after breathing out. Hips are only used for women.

    We'll estimate from your BMI, age and sex (Deurenberg, 1991). It's a rough guess and can be off by 5 points or more, especially if you're muscular. A quick tape measurement is better.

    Have smart-scale or body-comp numbers (fat in lb or kg)?

    From a Hume, InBody or similar scale. Enter total fat, or subcutaneous and visceral fat. Any of these counts as a measured body fat and is used instead of the estimate above.

    Health context · stays on this device

    Health context

    These answers change safety notes and limits. Education only, not medical advice.

    Do you take medication for blood pressure or blood sugar (including insulin)? Required

    Include insulin and any medicine that lowers blood sugar or blood pressure, whether it is for diabetes, weight or another condition. If you are unsure, ask your prescriber or pharmacist.

    From a recent blood test, in US units. They sharpen your threshold estimate and your body's story. They stay on this device.

    Waist goes under Basics. Measure midway between your lowest rib and the top of your hip bone, after a normal breath out, with the tape level.

    What these measurements can tell you

    A1c reflects your average glucose over about three months. It isn't an insulin-resistance score. A result in the diabetes range usually needs confirmation. Anemia, some hemoglobin variants, pregnancy and certain other conditions can make A1c less reliable. A treated A1c below 5.7% doesn't remove a previous diabetes diagnosis.

    Waist-to-height ratio describes central body size, not a measured visceral-fat volume. NICE uses 0.5 and 0.6 as rising central-adiposity risk bands for adults with a BMI under 35.

    Type 2 diabetes remission is a clinical outcome, not a promised weight-loss result: HbA1c below 6.5% for at least three months without the usual glucose-lowering medication, assessed by your clinician. This simulator doesn't forecast your A1c or remission.

    NIDDK: A1c test · NICE NG246: waist · Remission consensus

    How fast to gain
    Gain speed

    Lean: a small surplus to build the most muscle with the least fat. Your surplus is sized to an estimated muscle-gain rate for your training age and sex (practitioner rules of thumb from Lyle McDonald and Alan Aragon, not trial results), so treat these as estimates. Bigger surpluses mostly add fat (Garthe 2013; Iraki 2019; Helms 2023).

    Pace when there's no deadline
    Pace

    Maximal uses your full fat ceiling (about 31 kcal per lb of body fat a day). Steady uses about 60% of it, capped at a quarter of your daily burn.

    Lifting experience
    Lifting experience

    Advanced: muscle-gain rates used

    Estimated lean-mass gain with consistent, well-programmed lifting (4+ sessions a week, enough protein, enough food). These are estimates, not guarantees. Genetics, sleep, age and program quality move them a lot.

    Training ageMen / monthWomen / month

    Basis: practitioner models (McDonald; Aragon: beginners ~1–1.5% of body weight a month, intermediates ~0.5–1%, advanced ~0.25–0.5%) checked against review data (Iraki et al., 2019; Slater et al., 2019; Barakat et al., 2020). Women gain about the same relative amount as men (Roberts et al., 2020) but start with less muscle, so absolute gains are about half. Rates are trimmed for 2–3 sessions a week (×0.75), because fewer sessions usually means fewer hard sets per muscle (when weekly volume is equal, training a muscle 2 or 3+ times a week gives similar growth; Schoenfeld 2019), age 40+ (×0.85) and 60+ (×0.7), and taper as your fat-free mass index approaches a natural ceiling (about 25 for men and 21.5 for women; Kouri 1995). Beginners move to intermediate rates after 12 months. The lean-gain surplus is sized to these rates so that you add no more than about 0.8 lb of fat per lb of muscle. In a calorie deficit, gains shrink toward zero as the deficit nears your fat ceiling.

    Step 3 of 5

    Move

    Your typical week. Everyday steps count for more than most people think.

    Your typical week

    Steps per day

    Strength training

    Lifting is off. In a deficit, a bit more of the weight lost can be muscle, so keep protein high. The projection counts muscle gain only from lifting, so your actual body composition may differ. You can turn lifting back on any time.

    Strength training

    Minimalist, the minimum effective dose. Twice a week, do one set to failure each of a push (e.g. push-ups or a press), a pull (e.g. rows or pull-downs) and a leg movement (e.g. squats or leg press), using rest-pause: rest 10–20 seconds and keep going for a few more reps. It's a complete, sustainable habit that keeps your muscle in a deficit and builds it steadily, especially early on. Bigger programs add muscle faster.
    Evidence: in trained men a single set of 6–12 reps, 2–3 times a week, raised strength (Androulakis-Korakakis, Fisher & Steele 2020 meta-analysis). Reviews of minimal-dose training (Iversen, Norum, Schoenfeld & Fimland 2021, "No Time to Lift?"; Fyfe, Hamilton & Daly 2022) suggest about 4+ hard sets per muscle a week for growth. Muscle keeps growing with more weekly sets, with diminishing returns (Schoenfeld, Ogborn & Krieger 2017), so minimalist builds more slowly. Keeping muscle takes much less than building it (Bickel 2011). How much slower the model assumes is an estimate.

    Burn uses 2011 Compendium values, counting only what's above your resting burn. Afterburn (EPOC) after lifting adds roughly 5–15% of a session's burn, a few dozen kcal at most, so it's left out. Muscle gain follows how often and how hard you train each muscle: about 2 or more solid sessions a week reach the full rate for your level.

        Methods & references

        Fat ceiling. Alpert (2005) found that the fat store can release at most about 290 ± 25 kJ per kg of fat per day, which is 31.4 kcal per lb of fat. A deficit bigger than that is covered by liver glycogen (roughly 100 g, about 400 kcal, approximate) and by increasing protein loss from muscle and organs (these overlap). Intake can go at most 400 kcal a day below the fat ceiling deficit, no further (a design limit, not a published figure). To be conservative, the lean share of weight lost is multiplied by 1.15, so the model shows somewhat more muscle loss than the formulas alone would; that is an assumption, not a measurement. Each week's recommended deficit is set from that week's end-of-week fat mass, so it stays under the ceiling every day. Fat mass stores about 4,250 kcal per lb (≈ 9,400 kcal/kg, Hall 2008). That's not the 3,500 kcal/lb of adipose tissue. Together these give Alpert's response time of about 135 days. The ±25 kJ uncertainty is shown as a range.

        Daily burn. BMR from Mifflin-St Jeor (default) or Katch-McArdle, ×1.2 for sedentary daily living and digestion, then added activity on top. Steps above ~3,000 a day at about 0.5 kcal per kg per km (ACSM walking equation; stride ≈ 0.41 × height). Lifting at ~3 net METs and cardio at ~5 net METs (Ainsworth 2011 Compendium). Burn is recalculated every day as your weight and lean mass change.

        Metabolic adaptation. When you eat less, expenditure falls by more than tissue loss explains (adaptive thermogenesis; Rosenbaum & Leibel 2010; Fothergill 2016). The size is an assumption we chose, not a published constant: burn drops by about 14% of the cut in intake from your starting maintenance, building over about two weeks. The papers report the direction and rough size (holding a 10% lower weight lowered 24-hour expenditure about 20–25%, which is 10–15% below what tissue change explains; in the Biggest Loser follow-up the extra slowing was about 500 kcal a day at 6 years, with large differences between people), but not this coefficient. For a typical 500–700 kcal cut that's 70–100 kcal a day, roughly a 3–5% slowdown. If a fixed intake asks for more than your fat can supply, the body conserves harder (Keys 1950; Dulloo & Jacquet 1998; we did not read these two in full): extra adaptation covers the gap up to 25% of burn, and only the remainder comes from lean tissue. Recommended plans set each week's intake from this adapted burn, and adaptation stays in place while you hold a lower weight.

        Where losses come from. Inside the ceiling, the share of weight lost as lean tissue has two parts. The first follows Forbes' fat-dependent curve (leaner people lose more lean); resistance training (to ~0 with 4+ sessions a week) and adequate protein shrink it. The second is a structural share in larger bodies that training can't protect: the non-fat part of adipose tissue, skin, and load-bearing muscle. It rises from 0 at 18% body fat (men) / 28% (women) to 12% of weight lost at 38% / 48%, ×1.15 from age 60. Together, larger adults who lift lose about 10–18% of weight as lean, and about 20–25% without lifting (Villareal 2017; Weinheimer 2010). Energy beyond the ceiling that adaptation doesn't cover comes from lean tissue at ~1,800 kcal/kg. Gains: lean tissue costs ~2,500 kcal/kg including synthesis, up to the training-specific monthly rate (see Goal, Advanced). Any extra energy is stored as fat.

        Safety limits. Recommended intake never drops below 1,200 kcal (women) or 1,500 kcal (men) a day (NHLBI 1998). Body fat can't go below essential fat (5% men, 12% women), and results under 8% (men) or 18% (women) are flagged. Projections of a fixed intake (what you eat, or PSMF) stop when body fat reaches 8% / 18%, BMI drops below 18.5, or lean mass falls below 80% of where you started, and say why; they never extrapolate past those points. Week-one pace above 1.5% of body weight a week is flagged. Pregnancy and eating-disorder history change the plan or prompt a consult.

        Health context (optional). HbA1c bands follow ADA/NIDDK: under 5.7% is below the prediabetes range, 5.7–6.4% prediabetes, 6.5% or more the diabetes range, which needs clinical confirmation. Waist-to-height bands follow NICE NG246: 0.4–0.49 healthy, 0.5–0.59 increased and 0.6 or more high central adiposity, applied only below BMI 35. Type 2 diabetes remission is a clinical outcome, not a promised weight-loss result: HbA1c below 6.5% for at least three months without glucose-lowering medication (Riddle 2021). This tool doesn't forecast A1c, liver fat or remission. If you take glucose-lowering medication, or aren't sure, a medication card appears whenever the plan is a real deficit (250 kcal or more) or low-carb.

        PSMF. A protein-sparing modified fast is a short-term, clinician-supervised very-low-calorie diet. Protein is at least 1 g per lb (2.2 g/kg) of body weight; with high body fat (BMI 30+, or body fat above 30% for men / 40% for women) it's 1 g per lb of your goal weight or ideal body weight (Devine), your pick, with about 30 g carbohydrate and 15 g fat (Bistrian 1978; Chang & Kashyap 2014). It's suggested only as a gentle note when what you eat is 1,000 kcal or less (for a food log, after you tap Done adding foods), usually reserved for BMI 30+ (27+ with weight-related conditions), and projected with the same stop rules.

        Protein. 1 g per lb (2.2 g per kg) for anyone who lifts or is gaining. In Morton 2018's meta-analysis the extra muscle from more protein leveled off at about 1.6 g/kg a day on average, with the upper confidence limit near 2.2 g/kg, so 2.2 covers nearly everyone (Morton 2018; Jäger 2017). Lean lifters in a deficit may do better higher still: 2.3–3.1 g per kg of lean mass (Helms, Zinn et al. 2014; Helms, Aragon et al. 2014). Spreading it over 3–4 or more meals of about 0.4 g/kg each is a sensible pattern (Schoenfeld & Aragon 2018). Intakes well above this (3.4–4.4 g/kg) were safe and did not add fat in short trials in trained lifters (Antonio 2014, 2015, 2016), but they aren't needed for muscle. Without lifting: 2.2 for maximal fat loss, 2.0 for other fat loss and recomposition, 1.6 for maintenance. With high body fat (BMI 30 or more, or body fat above 30% for men or 40% for women), protein is based on 1 g per lb of your goal weight or of your ideal body weight (Devine), whichever you choose, never on total weight. Otherwise, above ~25% (men) or ~32% (women) body fat it uses your lean mass at a healthy body fat (18% men, 28% women). PSMF keeps its own rule. Fat is about 25–30% of calories (at least 0.5 g/kg of the reference weight), and carbs fill the rest.

        Keep my body fat % (default for lean gain). The surplus is sized so that fat makes up your starting body-fat percentage of every pound gained (fat gain = BF% × total gain), so body fat stays at or near where it started (within about 0.5 points). The surplus covers your training-limited muscle gain plus that small amount of fat, for example about 50 kcal a day for an intermediate man at 10% body fat. Your muscle-gain rate therefore sets the timeline: 145 → 155 lb at 10% takes about 9 months for an intermediate lifting 4+ times a week and longer for advanced lifters. This assumes a small, steady surplus is enough to support the full training-limited rate, which is an optimistic but common practitioner assumption. If a target, a body-fat cap (keep % or a ceiling) and a deadline can't all fit, the simulator says how long it really takes and offers two one-click fixes: use that many weeks, or allow the body fat needed to make your date. It never stops short of the target silently.

        Gaining weight. "Let it rise slowly" is the v4 lean bulk. The surplus is sized to your estimated muscle-gain rate (training age, sex, sessions per week, age, and how close you are to a natural fat-free-mass ceiling), so you add no more than about 0.8 lb of fat per lb of muscle: roughly 300 kcal a day for a male beginner lifting 4+ times a week, 150 for an intermediate, and 75–100 for an advanced lifter (Iraki 2019; Slater 2019; Helms 2023). If a deadline is too short to gain mostly muscle, the simulator says so and shows the realistic timeline instead of filling the gap with fat. "Faster (more fat)" roughly doubles the surplus (300–600 kcal) for hard gainers or people who are underweight, and the projection shows the extra fat. An optional body-fat ceiling stops the plan where you'd cross it. Muscle gain is an estimate: genetics, sleep and program quality change it a lot. The model treats every surplus calorie alike. In trained lifters, extra calories eaten as protein (3.4–4.4 g/kg a day, several hundred kcal more) did not raise fat mass in trials lasting a few months (Antonio 2014, 2015, 2016), so with very high protein the projected fat gain may be too high.

        Body fat estimates. U.S. Navy tape equations (Hodgdon & Beckett 1984, about ±3–4 points). BMI-based formula when nothing else is available (Deurenberg 1991, about ±5 points). FFMI = lean kg ÷ height m², normalized to 1.8 m (Kouri 1995). Waist-to-height under 0.5 is the healthy cut-off (Ashwell 2012).

        Body figure. Where WebGL is available, the figure is a 3D body built from the CC0 MakeHuman base mesh, with a neutral smooth face, form-fitting athletic wear that follows the body (compression shorts, plus a sports bra for women; men can switch off "Shirtless" for a fitted compression tank) and a skin tone you pick. Shape targets for subcutaneous fat, belly, hips and thighs, arms and chest, lower-belly apron and flanks, and muscle are solved so the body's volume matches your fat and lean mass (fat 0.9 kg/L, lean 1.1 kg/L). Your ancestry answer never changes how the figure looks. See the fat shows muscle in red under a translucent yellow layer whose strength follows the fat thickness at each point. A window into the abdomen shows the estimated fat around the organs (to scale with its estimated volume) and a liver that turns from red-brown to tan as its estimated fat rises. The organ shapes are simplified drawings, not anatomy.

        Where you carry it. Your answers set a score from "mostly under the skin" (pinchable, hyperplastic: hips, thighs, arms, flanks, a lower-belly apron; little fat around the organs) to "mostly around the organs" (metabolic: a firm, round belly with more visceral and liver fat). It's nudged by type 2 diabetes, prediabetes or an HbA1c of 5.7% or more and by fatty liver, all tied to visceral and liver fat (Taylor & Holman 2015; Neeland 2012; Fabbrini 2010). A waist large for your height and BMI is a central-fat marker (Ashwell 2012). Age (Kuk 2009) and menopause (Lovejoy 2008) also count, and so do your own description and, when there's no description, your photo's shape. Ancestry is optional and gives small, evidence-based nudges only. On average, South Asian and East/Southeast Asian adults carry more visceral fat at the same BMI (Lear 2007; Raji 2001; Wulan 2010), which is why the ADA recommends diabetes screening from BMI 23 for Asian Americans and why equivalent-risk BMIs are lower (Ntuk 2014). Hispanic/Latino adults have more liver fat on average (Browning 2004). Black/African-ancestry adults have less visceral and more subcutaneous fat at the same waist (Carroll 2008; Katzmarzyk 2010). Fat is split into visceral, belly-subcutaneous, hip-and-thigh, arm/chest/back and other depots. Men carry about twice the visceral share of women at the same fat mass, and the visceral share eases at very high fat mass.

        Progress photos (v6.3). Check-in photos you add under See it on your photo are tagged with the week you're at. The newest one restarts the rest of the projection from your entered weight and body fat (or from the plan's values for that week if you leave them blank), with the same goal, food and training, and any deadline or time window shortened by the weeks already done. Photos are shrunk and kept only in this browser (IndexedDB) until you remove them; export and import use a JSON file you control.

        Where you gain it first (v6.3). For gain goals (lean gain, build muscle, a higher target weight) the regional section shows where things go on instead. New lean mass (mostly muscle) goes where you train; with full-body lifting it is split by where skeletal muscle sits, about 55% legs and glutes and 45% upper body for men (60/40 for women; Janssen 2000), an estimate. Fat that comes with a gain follows the same power-law pattern in reverse, so it returns first to your usual storage areas: the belly and around the organs for most men, the hips and thighs for women before menopause and the belly after (Karpe & Pinnick 2015; Lovejoy 2008). Recomposition shows fat coming off and muscle going on together.

        Where you lose it first. Each depot follows a power law of the engine's total fat mass (after Hallgreen & Hall 2008), so the before, week-N and goal figures all come from the same trajectory. Visceral fat falls about 1.6–1.7× faster than total fat early on, and the gap narrows with larger losses (Chaston & Dixon 2008). In kilograms, most of the fat lost still comes from under the skin (Merlotti 2017). Hip and thigh fat is the most stubborn, especially in women (Karpe & Pinnick 2015). Liver fat falls fastest (Lim 2011) and is only drawn, not reported as a number. All of these are population-average estimates, not measurements. DEXA or MRI can measure them.

        Fat pattern: medical facts first (v5). The "where you carry it" score blends signals, with medical facts weighted more than self-report. Type 2 diabetes or an A1c of 6.5% or more pushes strongly toward fat around the organs (+0.8); prediabetes or an A1c of 5.7–6.4% moderately (+0.4); fatty liver +0.4. High body fat or BMI with a normal A1c and no diabetes points to mostly under-the-skin fat (−0.35, or −0.5 at BMI 35+ / body fat 35%+ men, 43%+ women). Waist-to-height ratio adds its own term, and 0.6 or more (a waist over 60% of your height) adds +0.25 toward organ fat (NICE NG246). Your own answers and a photo still count, at 0.6× when medical facts are present. The one-line "why" names the strongest reason.

        Cardio types (v5). Burn = net MET × body weight (kg) × hours, where net MET is the 2011 Compendium value minus 1 (the resting part is already in your daily burn). Easy / moderate / hard: walking 2.8 / 3.5 / 5.0; incline walking 5.3 / 6.5 / 8.0 (moderate interpolated); cycling 4.8 / 6.8 / 8.8; running 8.3 / 9.8 / 11.0; rowing 4.8 / 7.0 / 8.5; swimming 5.8 / 8.3 / 9.8; HIIT 4.3 / 8.0 / 9.0; sports 4.0 / 6.0 / 8.0. In Advanced, cardio can be entered by average heart rate (Keytel 2005), by pace (ACSM walking and running equations) or as watch calories, which are used as given (watches often overestimate).

        Advanced mode (v5). Lifting style, hard sets per week (default 10) and how close sets go to failure scale the muscle-gain rate modestly (0.5–1.2×: more weekly sets build more muscle, with diminishing returns past about 10; Schoenfeld 2017; Pelland 2026. Training closer to failure helps a little; Refalo 2023; Robinson 2024) and the lifting burn. A measured resting burn or total burn calibrates day 0 (the model keeps its adaptation from there). DEXA body fat replaces the estimate. Manual macros as % split the day's target; as grams they become what you eat. Refeed days set intake to maintenance on the last 1–2 days of each week of a fat-loss plan, which slows it honestly (Byrne 2018).

        Anatomy views (v6). Under the figure, Body is the default; Fat + muscle peels the fat under the skin off one side to show the muscle; Inside opens a window into the abdomen showing fat around the organs (yellow lobules over the gut), the liver and the fat layer; Muscle hides the fat. Everything is driven by the same fat-pattern engine as the rest of the plan: visceral fat in kg, fat under the skin, and liver fat (%) for each body, now and at goal, so the visceral and liver fat visibly fall first (visceral about 1.6× faster than fat under the skin early on; hips and thighs last; Merlotti 2017, Hallgreen & Hall 2008). Liver fat is graded with MRI-PDFF bands (under 5% normal, 5–17.4% mild, 17.4–22.1% moderate, above 22.1% severe; Tang 2013); the liver turns patchy, mottled pale yellow-tan with fine fat droplets as it rises (steatosis), and fat around the organs is drawn as lobules with fine septa and vessels. When zoomed in (+, Close-up, pinch or Ctrl + scroll), dragging moves the view; Move switches drag between moving and rotating (Shift-drag does the other) and Reset recenters. Teal dots show glycogen (stored carbohydrate) in muscle and liver: fuller with more carbohydrate per kg of lean mass, lower in the liver during a deficit, and blunted by liver fat (insulin resistance; Shulman 1990). These are illustrations from your estimates, not a scan. Organs are generated in code (no scanned or Z-Anatomy meshes).

        Diabetes status from A1c (v6). If you leave the diabetes question unanswered and enter an A1c, the answer is set from it (6.5% or more: diabetes, assumed type 2; 5.7–6.4%: prediabetes; under 5.7%: no diabetes) with a note, and you can change it. If you answered and your A1c points elsewhere, your answer is kept and a gentle note says so. A result in the diabetes range needs clinical confirmation; a treated A1c below the range doesn't remove a diagnosis.

        Lifting (v6). Quick choices: None, Minimalist, 2–3 or 4+ a week. Minimalist is the minimum effective dose: twice a week, one rest-pause set to failure each of a push, a pull and a leg movement (about 10–20 minutes). It keeps muscle in a deficit about as well as 2–3 full sessions and builds it at roughly 55–75% of their rate (a model estimate, not a trial result), with little calorie burn. Sources: Androulakis-Korakakis 2020 (single sets raise strength in trained men), Iversen 2021 and Fyfe 2022 (minimal-dose reviews; about 4+ weekly sets per muscle for growth), Bickel 2011 (retention needs much less volume); Schoenfeld 2017 shows the volume dose-response (more sets, more growth) rather than a minimum dose. Advanced adds Custom rows like cardio: type (heavy strength, hypertrophy, circuit / CrossFit-style, bodyweight, machines, Minimalist), effort, minutes a session and days a week. Burn = days × minutes × (Compendium MET − 1) × kg (2011 Compendium 02020–02054; e.g. vigorous resistance training 6.0, moderate 3.5–5.0, circuit 8.0). Afterburn (EPOC) adds only about 5–15% of a session's burn, so it is left out. Each row adds a weekly training stimulus (sessions × type × effort × session length); about 2+ solid sessions a week per muscle reach the full gain rate for your level, fewer give less, and none gives no gain and more lean loss in a deficit. A separate retention score weights intensity, since keeping muscle needs much less volume than building it. With custom rows, the Advanced style / sets / reps-in-reserve settings are not applied (no double counting).

        Smoother figure (v6). Fat growth is diffused across the mesh before use, so regions blend into each other instead of meeting at creases, and the belly grows round rather than pointed; the chest is kept smooth and neutral. A light volume-preserving smoothing pass runs on the shown surface, stronger at higher body fat. Volumes are re-measured after smoothing so the figure still matches your fat and lean mass.

        Exact goals and your daily calorie target (v6.4). On Maximal or Steady fat loss you can enter an exact goal weight or goal body fat % in the Exact goal box right under the goal cards (it scrolls into view and lights up when you pick a goal). The plan then runs to that target at the goal's pace: Maximal uses your full fat ceiling, Steady about 60% of it. The Food step shows one number, Your daily calorie target: your daily burn minus the deficit (or plus the surplus). Tap How we got this for the breakdown. Once you enter foods or turn on Simulate what I actually eat, a line shows how many calories you're eating and how far over or under your target that is; with simulate on, the projection follows what you eat.

        Softer, more realistic fat (v6.1). On heavier figures fat is shaped as smooth volume with wide, gradual falloffs, so there are no ledges or angled edges at the belly, flanks or back. A soft gravity fold forms under the lower belly as body fat rises (more with softer fat and after 50), with a gentle roll at the sides and back, and the hips fill out in step with the waist. Where fat is thick the surface is finer and smoothed (muscle definition on lean bodies is unchanged), and skin folds are softly shaded. The figure is an illustration from your estimates, not a scan.

        Muscle definition and close-up (v5). Visible abdominal definition is drawn as a soft, procedural shading map (not anatomy scanned from a person), faded in by body fat: men full at about 10–12%, softer at 12–15%, none by about 17%; women full at about 17–18%, softer to about 20–23%, none by about 25%, scaled by muscularity. It's illustrative. Real definition varies with genetics, water and lighting. Pinch, Ctrl/⌘ + scroll, double-click or the Close-up button zoom the torso.

        Build muscle (max) (v5). A moderate 250–350 kcal a day surplus sized by training age and sex: men about 350 / 300 / 250 kcal and women about 300 / 275 / 250 kcal for under 1 year / 1–3 years / 3+ years of lifting. It steps down as you gain experience over the projection and never goes below 250 (Iraki 2019: roughly 10–20% above maintenance for newer lifters, less once trained; Helms 2023: small surpluses build about as much muscle as large ones, with less fat). Muscle grows only as fast as your estimated gain rate allows, so the rest of the surplus is stored as fat, and the projection shows that fat rise. Without lifting there's no surplus. "See the muscle" shows the fat-free surface, which grows with projected lean mass.

        Example days (v5). Four diet types × five styles (Everyday, Quick & easy, Vegetarian, Plant-based, Gluten-free), built from rounded USDA FoodData Central values. Each type sets calorie shares: Balanced keeps protein at 15–35% and fat at 25–35%; Lower carb about 20% carbs; Higher protein at least 35% protein; Low fat about 18% fat. Your protein target is kept within each type's range. Portions are solved in usable steps to land within about 5% of the calories and on the macro targets. Allergens are listed from the foods used. The Gluten-free style uses only naturally gluten-free foods (oats only if labeled gluten-free), with a reminder that people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should check labels for cross-contamination.

        Saved days (v5). Saved days live only in this browser (localStorage). Export and Import move them as a .json file. Nothing is uploaded.

        Before you set Move and Food. On the Goal step the projection assumes 2–3 lifting sessions a week and adequate protein, and says so. Once you reach the Move and Food steps, your own choices replace those assumptions everywhere, including the live summary.

        Food search. Branded products come from Open Food Facts (searched from your browser; barcodes by number or camera where the browser supports it). Generic foods come from USDA FoodData Central. Values are per serving as listed by the source, or per 100 g. Your day log adds up calories and macros; once it reaches 500 kcal it becomes the intake used in the simulation, until you type a number yourself. Database values can be wrong or out of date, so check the label.

        Your 3D from a photo. With a chest-to-hips (torso) or head-to-feet photo, a pose model (MediaPipe Pose Landmarker, run entirely in your browser) finds your joints and outline. We measure outline widths at the chest, waist, navel, hips and thighs as fractions of your height (and depths from an optional side photo), (a torso photo uses the shoulder-to-hip distance for scale and measures the chest, waist and navel only, so the legs keep the typical shape), then adjust three fat-distribution settings of the figure (upper body, hips and thighs, belly) until the figure's outline, measured the same way, matches. The figure's total volume still comes from your entered weight and body fat, so the photo changes only where it carries fat. On test renders it recovers the outline within about 1 cm on average; real photos are less exact (clothing, posture, camera angle), so treat it as an approximation. The photo is not uploaded.

        You at week N. The week picker on the results shows the projected composition at any week, as a 3D figure (free, on your device) and, optionally, as an AI illustration of your photo. The AI image is an illustration of those numbers, not a prediction.

        Educational tool, not medical advice. Full disclaimer · The science · These are estimates from population research. Your results will differ. Using this tool doesn't create a patient relationship. If you're pregnant or breastfeeding, under 18, have diabetes, heart, kidney or liver disease, take prescription medicines, or have a history of disordered eating, talk with your clinician before changing how you eat or train.

        Before you continue

        BMI isn't perfect. It doesn't separate muscle from fat, so it can misread very muscular or very small-framed people. Still, losing more weight from here can affect bone, hormones, energy and immunity. Please talk with your clinician before further weight loss. The plan keeps its safety calorie floor either way.
